items.title: Q4 Outlook for Traders: Three tests for the wall of worry.
items.excerpt: One of the lessons markets have delivered repeatedly in recent years is that an impressive backdrop of risks does not deliver logical market outcomes. The Iran war produced the largest disruption to global energy supplies in decades. Long-term government bond yields have pushed to levels not seen in many years, while the extraordinary AI investment boom has reached a scale that increasingly invites difficult questions about how the spending will eventually generate adequate returns. And yet global equities, outside of some spectacular volatility in the most crowded parts of the AI trade, have again shown an extraordinary ability to climb the proverbial wall of worry. That resilience deserves respect. Investors have been conditioned by years of buying market weakness, while enormous…

items.title: Q4 Outlook for Investors: Raise the bar
items.excerpt: Our Q4 base case is a volatile upward grind, but with much greater dispersion beneath the index. Key points: AI meets expensive money: AI spending can remain strong, but higher funding costs, rapid obsolescence and rising reinvestment needs will increasingly separate companies that can comfortably finance the AI race from those spending simply to stay competitive. Inflation needs more than one hedge: Oil is only part of the risk. El Ni o, fiscal spending and the AI infrastructure buildout could also keep pressure on food, power, commodities and bond yields. Bonds are competitive again: With the US 10-year Treasury yield around 5%, investors no longer need to rely as heavily on equities for returns. They should assess whether recent strong stock-market gains have pushed portfolios away…

items.title: Euro futures drop 2.5% as markets look to jobs data.
items.excerpt: Euro FX futures continued to decline through the end of September, closing out the month with a loss of over 2.5%. The currency struggled as sustained dollar strength pushed prices to a new year-to-date low close, settling at 1.1330. As prices have moved lower, the CVOL Index has indicated steadily rising volatility across the market. Looking ahead, traders turn their focus to the labor market, with Thursday's Challenger job cuts and jobless claims leading into Friday's critical nonfarm payrolls report.

items.title: Bonds 101: A simple investor guide to navigating today’s higher yields
items.excerpt: Higher yields have made bonds relevant again, with the right role depending on an investor’s life stage, income needs and tolerance for interest-rate and inflation risk. Key points: Bond yields have risen sharply , making fixed income more relevant again for investors seeking income, diversification or greater portfolio stability. The opportunity is not simply a call that yields have peaked. Higher starting yields mean investors can earn more income while taking a more measured view on interest rates. But higher yields do not necessarily mean it is time to go all-in on long-duration bonds. Inflation, oil prices, government borrowing and further Federal Reserve tightening could keep yields elevated or push them higher still. Why bonds are back in the conversation Bond yields have risen…

items.title: Euro futures drop to lowest level since mid-July as dollar gains.
items.excerpt: Euro futures traded lower, reaching 1.1350 before closing near 1.1365, marking the lowest level since mid-July. The decline was driven by U.S. dollar strength following rising inflation expectations and shifting Federal Reserve rate hike expectations. The euro has fallen approximately 3% since its August peak above 1.17. Meanwhile, option-derived volatility increased alongside the market decline, as measured by the CVOL index. Speculators expanded their net short positions last week, extending a continuous net short posture in euro futures since late June.

items.title: British Pound futures bounce as UK consumer confidence hits 2-year high.
items.excerpt: British Pound futures rebounded to close out the week following improved UK consumer confidence and hawkish signals from the Bank of England. After finishing higher in just two of the previous 11 sessions, the pound saw a lift as short covering emerged ahead of the weekend. Support also materialized as UK consumer confidence unexpectedly jumped to a two-year high, with GfK's index rising to minus 13 for September. Market expectations shifted as Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden and Governor Andrew Bailey highlighted inflation risks, noting that elevated energy costs could make it increasingly difficult to hold rates steady and leaving further rate hikes on the table.

items.title: Crude's supply risks meet a 66.4% probability of a Fed hike.
items.excerpt: The week of Sept. 28 brings a critical slate of economic data, central bank developments, and energy market catalysts. Traders will monitor Strait of Hormuz discussions and an upcoming OPEC+ meeting for immediate impacts on WTI Crude Oil futures. Attention also shifts to the U.S., where July PCE and August Nonfarm Payrolls will provide the latest view on inflation and hiring ahead of the October FOMC meeting. The CME FedWatch Tool currently reflects a 66.4% probability of another rate hike. Alongside a busy macroeconomic calendar featuring PMIs and inflation figures from across the globe, the earnings schedule offers updates from 18 large-cap companies, including Micron Technology and Nike.

items.title: Has the era of cheap food come to an end?
items.excerpt: From climate shocks, including the effects of El Niño, and rising labour costs to changing welfare standards and technological innovation, food prices may be entering a new structural regime. In this episode, Heidi Richardson and Sreedhar Mahamkali from UBS Research discuss the forces driving this shift, the potential role of technology as a counterbalance, and what a structurally higher food inflation environment could mean for consumers, businesses and markets. *(This information is subject to a disclaimer at the end of this podcast. Please ensure that you listen to the disclaimer and go to www.ubs.com for further information about UBS).

items.title: Australian Dollar futures drop to 2-month lows as Fed speakers turn hawkish.
items.excerpt: Dan Deming outlines the recent price action across major FX markets, noting that Australian Dollar futures have traded lower for a third consecutive session to reach two-month lows near the 0.7020 level. Deming explains that hawkish comments from Federal Reserve speakers regarding higher interest rates, combined with stronger-than-expected economic data, have bolstered the U.S. dollar and pressured foreign currencies. He also examines the broader impact on the currency space, highlighting that Euro futures are trading at two-month lows while the British Pound has fallen to levels not seen since early June, as rising U.S. yields continue to weigh on the FX complex.

U.S.-China trade talks resume in Washington, delivering an immediate extension of the existing trade truce into January. Crude oil surges past $94 following a strike in the Strait of Hormuz and elevated geopolitical risk in the Middle East, overshadowing inventory data. The data calendar focuses on the 7-Year Treasury note auction, earnings reports from Costco and Tamboran Resources, U.S. durable goods orders and University of Michigan sentiment.
